problems.form_value: randomized 'yes' and criterion_1 'met', on the quote 'Human participants were randomly assigned to one of three treatments' (PDF p. 9). The HumanPlusAI arm description says 'The Prolific description for this arm requested people who already had an OpenAI or Bard account.' The form leaves the conflict to eligibility.reason and open_questions.
problems.source_says: The random-assignment sentence is in the text, but the document does not show that HumanPlusAI and HumanBaseline writers came from one randomized pool. The account request sits in the Prolific description, which people read before they enroll. Either it applied to every writer, and the form's 'for this arm' is wrong, or it applied to HumanPlusAI only, and those writers were screened on owning an AI account while HumanBaseline writers were not. The paper states the request only in the HumanPlusAI item and calls the writers a representative sample of US adults, which fits the second reading. Footnote 3's per-arm Prolific targets and overshoots (700, 300, 300 aimed; 702, 304, 315 received) are easier to square with separate recruitment but do not prove it. The paper never says which reading holds. The AEA registry entry (AEARCTR-0011584) or the supplementary materials may settle it.

problems.form_value: All 309 declared a tool (footnote 4). The paper reports no measure of actual use.
problems.source_says: Minor wording. No coded value changes. Footnote 4 and the Table 3 title label the counts 'AI used', not declarations. The only instrument the paper describes is the declaration before writing, which offered 'None'. Footnote 4 lists no 'None', and the paper does not say what happened to writers who chose it (315 complete responses, 309 analyzed). Suggested wording: 'Footnote 4 and Table 3 report AI used: Bard 39, ChatGPT-3.5 184, ChatGPT-4 86 (sum 309). The paper describes only a declaration before writing and no check of actual use.'
problems.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 8), HumanPlusAI item and footnote 4; PDF p. 16 (printed p. 14), Table 3 title; PDF p. 9 (printed p. 7), footnote 3

confirmed.statement: The document states random assignment of writers. The form's quote 'Human participants were randomly assigned to one of three treatments' is verbatim, and its locator is right.

What was assigned is AI access for the writer's own text. HumanPlusAI writers 'had the choice to utilize Bard or ChatGPT (3.5 or 4) for help in producing their responses' and declared a tool (ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, Bard, or None) before writing. The introduction says they 'were instructed to use them when generating the answers'. Raters scored that text, so the arms do not differ only in whose output is evaluated.
confirmed.locator: PDF p. 10 (printed p. 8), Section 2.1.1, HumanPlusAI item; PDF p. 5 (printed p. 3), Introduction

confirmed.statement: The tools are generative AI. The paper calls ChatGPT and Bard 'generative AI chatbots' and names ChatGPT among large language models. role open_chat fits free use of a chatbot.

summary: The PDF supports the form on what was assigned, the tools, the no-AI comparison arm, and the between-subjects design: writers 'were randomly assigned' to three treatments, HumanPlusAI writers could use ChatGPT-3.5, ChatGPT-4, or Bard for their own text, and HumanBaseline writers worked 'autonomously' (PDF pp. 9-10). But the HumanPlusAI item says the Prolific description asked for existing OpenAI or Bard account holders (PDF p. 10), which, with per-arm Prolific targets (footnote 3) and the claim of a representative US sample, points to separate recruitment or screening of the AI arm, so the document does not show that AI and no-AI writers came from one randomized pool.
